results.name: singleton_near_far_gradient
results.description: For single-example sets, yes rate to targets within 10 of the example minus yes rate to targets more than 10 away; observed above null means people generalise more locally (steeper similarity gradient) than the model predicts, below means flatter.
results.code:
# name: singleton_near_far_gradient
# description: For single-example sets, yes rate to targets within 10 of the example minus yes rate to targets more than 10 away; observed above null means people generalise more locally (steeper similarity gradient) than the model predicts, below means flatter.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    single = ~s.str.contains(",")
    x = pd.to_numeric(s.where(single, "0"), errors="coerce").fillna(0).astype(int).values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].values
    d = np.abs(t - x)
    near = single.values & (d <= 10) & (d > 0)
    far = single.values & (d > 10)
    if near.sum() == 0 or far.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[near].mean() - r[far].mean())

results.name: prime_set_odd_composite_yes_rate
results.description: After sets of 2+ examples that are all odd primes (not all ending in the same digit), yes rate to odd composite targets more than 5 from every example; observed above null means the model's prime-over-odd shift over-suppresses the "odd numbers" reading, below means it under-suppresses it.
results.code:
# name: prime_set_odd_composite_yes_rate
# description: After sets of 2+ examples that are all odd primes (not all ending in the same digit), yes rate to odd composite targets more than 5 from every example; observed above null means the model's prime-over-odd shift over-suppresses the "odd numbers" reading, below means it under-suppresses it.
def test_statistic(df):
    pr = np.zeros(102, dtype=bool)
    for k in range(2, 101):
        pr[k] = all(k % j for j in range(2, int(k ** 0.5) + 1))
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").reindex(columns=range(4)).values
    ok = ~np.isnan(ex)
    exi = np.where(ok, ex, 0).astype(int)
    n = ok.sum(1)
    allp = np.all(~ok | (pr[exi] & (exi % 2 == 1)), axis=1)
    last = np.where(ok, exi % 10, -1)
    same_last = np.all((last == last[:, [0]]) | ~ok, axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    dist = np.min(np.where(ok, np.abs(exi - t[:, None]), 1000), axis=1)
    m = (n >= 2) & allp & ~same_last & (t % 2 == 1) & ~pr[t] & (t > 1) & (dist > 5)
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].values[m].mean())

results.name: trial_index_yes_slope
results.description: OLS slope of the yes response on standardized trial_index across all trials; observed below null means yes rate declines over the session more than the (stationary) model predicts, above means it rises.

results.name: gcd2_far_even_yes_rate
results.description: For sets of 2+ all-even examples whose gcd is exactly 2 and not sharing a final digit, yes rate to even non-example targets more than 10 from every example; observed above null means the model under-predicts "even numbers" generalisation, below means it over-predicts it.
results.code:
# name: gcd2_far_even_yes_rate
# description: For sets of 2+ all-even examples whose gcd is exactly 2 and not sharing a final digit, yes rate to even non-example targets more than 10 from every example; observed above null means the model under-predicts "even numbers" generalisation, below means it over-predicts it.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").reindex(columns=range(4)).values
    ok = ~np.isnan(ex)
    exi = np.where(ok, ex, 0).astype(int)
    n = ok.sum(1)
    g = np.gcd.reduce(exi, axis=1)
    last = np.where(ok, exi % 10, -1)
    same_last = np.all((last == last[:, [0]]) | ~ok, axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    dist = np.min(np.where(ok, np.abs(exi - t[:, None]), 1000), axis=1)
    m = (n >= 2) & (g == 2) & ~same_last & (t % 2 == 0) & (dist > 10)
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].values[m].mean())

results.name: far_target_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate to targets more than 30 away from every example in sets of 2+ examples whose examples do not all share parity; observed above null means the model under-predicts diffuse/broad yes responses (e.g. rejects too strongly), below means it over-predicts them via lapse or broad rules.
results.code:
# name: far_target_yes_rate
# description: Yes rate to targets more than 30 away from every example in sets of 2+ examples whose examples do not all share parity; observed above null means the model under-predicts diffuse/broad yes responses (e.g. rejects too strongly), below means it over-predicts them via lapse or broad rules.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").reindex(columns=range(4)).values
    ok = ~np.isnan(ex)
    exi = np.where(ok, ex, 0).astype(int)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    n = ok.sum(1)
    par = np.where(ok, exi % 2, -1)
    n_odd = (par == 1).sum(1)
    mixed = (n_odd > 0) & (n_odd < n)
    dist = np.min(np.where(ok, np.abs(exi - t[:, None]), 1000), axis=1)
    m = (n >= 2) & mixed & (dist > 30)
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].values[m].mean())

results.name: digit_reversal_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate among trials whose target is the digit-reversal of a two-digit, non-repdigit example (and not itself an example); observed above the model's null mean means people treat reversed numerals as same-program members more than the rule/interval model predicts.
results.code:
# name: digit_reversal_yes_rate
# description: Yes rate among trials whose target is the digit-reversal of a two-digit, non-repdigit example (and not itself an example); observed above the model's null mean means people treat reversed numerals as same-program members more than the rule/interval model predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
    ex = ex.reindex(columns=range(4))
    tv = t.values
    rev_hit = np.zeros(len(df), dtype=bool)
    is_ex = np.zeros(len(df), dtype=bool)
    for c in range(4):
        x = ex[c].values
        ok = ~np.isnan(x)
        xi = np.where(ok, x, 0).astype(int)
        r = (xi % 10) * 10 + xi // 10
        valid = ok & (xi >= 10) & (xi <= 99) & (xi % 11 != 0) & (xi % 10 != 0)
        rev_hit |= valid & (r == tv)
        is_ex |= ok & (xi == tv)
    m = rev_hit & ~is_ex
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].values[m].mean())

results.name: within_range_setsize_contrast
results.description: Yes rate to non-example targets lying strictly between the min and max example for 4-example sets minus the same for 2-example sets; observed above null means larger sets fill in their range more than the model predicts (weaker size-principle tightening), below means more.
results.code:
# name: within_range_setsize_contrast
# description: Yes rate to non-example targets lying strictly between the min and max example for 4-example sets minus the same for 2-example sets; observed above null means larger sets fill in their range more than the model predicts (weaker size-principle tightening), below means more.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").reindex(columns=range(4)).values
    ok = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = ok.sum(1)
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1)
    hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    is_ex = np.any(ok & (ex == t[:, None]), axis=1)
    inside = (t > lo) & (t < hi) & ~is_ex
    r = df["rating"].values
    a = inside & (n == 4)
    b = inside & (n == 2)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: common_contained_digit_yes_rate
results.description: For sets of 2+ examples that all contain a common digit d but do not all end in the same digit, the yes rate to non-example targets containing d whose distance to the nearest example exceeds 5; observed above null means the model under-weights "contains digit d" rules.
results.code:
# name: common_contained_digit_yes_rate
# description: For sets of 2+ examples that all contain a common digit d but do not all end in the same digit, the yes rate to non-example targets containing d whose distance to the nearest example exceeds 5; observed above null means the model under-weights "contains digit d" rules.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    ex = s.str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").reindex(columns=range(4)).values
    ok = ~np.isnan(ex)
    exi = np.where(ok, ex, -1000).astype(int)
    n = ok.sum(1)
    sel = np.zeros(len(df), dtype=bool)
    last = np.where(ok, exi % 10, -1)
    same_last = np.all((last == last[:, [0]]) | ~ok, axis=1)
    for d in range(10):
        has = np.zeros_like(ok)
        for c in range(4):
            col = exi[:, c]
            has[:, c] = ok[:, c] & (((col % 10) == d) | (((col // 10) % 10 == d) & (col >= 10)) | ((col == 100) & (d in (0, 1))))
        all_has = np.all(has | ~ok, axis=1) & (n >= 2) & ~same_last
        tc = ((t % 10) == d) | (((t // 10) % 10 == d) & (t >= 10)) | ((t == 100) & (d in (0, 1)))
        sel |= all_has & tc
    dist = np.min(np.where(ok, np.abs(exi - t[:, None]), 1000), axis=1)
    m = sel & (dist > 5)
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].values[m].mean())
